title: Did the Dutch trade Manhattan for nutmeg?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with baseball small talk and a riff on "homogenocene," the homogenization of the planet since the Age of Exploration, which they trace back to Ottoman Sultan Mehmed the Second's capture of Constantinople and the resulting closure of Silk Road trade routes. They discuss why spices were valuable in Europe, the rise of the Portuguese spice trade, and the Dutch and English East India companies. Henry Hudson's voyage leads to the Dutch claim on Manhattan, the disputed 1626 purchase by Peter Minuit (the sixty guilders and the Manhattan name legend), and the Dutch colony of New Netherland. The episode then turns to nutmeg in the Banda Islands, the Dutch monopoly and the brutal conquest of the islanders, Run island and British rivalry, and Jan Pieterszoon Coen's burning of nutmeg trees. The Treaty of Breda (1667) gave England Manhattan in exchange for Run and other concessions, and the Dutch retook it in 1673 before the Treaty of Westminster (1674) returned it. A listener mail segment about Robert De Niro tipping a hotel doorman closes the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and homogenocene
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with baseball small talk, then Josh introduces the term 'homogenocene' coined by Michael Samways and described by Charles C. Mann, tracing global homogenization back to Mehmed the Second's capture of Constantinople.

segments.title: Ottoman conquest, Silk Road and the Age of Exploration
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Ottoman control of Constantinople cut European access to Middle Eastern and Asian trade routes, pushing Europeans to sea. They note many discoveries were accidental, and describe Vasco da Gama's successful route around Africa that gave Portugal dominance of trade.

segments.title: Why spices mattered
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain the European demand for exotic spices, their use to mask spoiled food, their status as a sign of nobility, their medicinal uses, and peppercorn as a form of rent.

segments.title: Dutch and English East India companies
segments.summary: The Dutch and English form chartered trading companies to compete with Portugal in the spice trade. The Dutch East India Company (VOC) and the English East India Company are described, along with their brutality and competition in the East Indies.

segments.title: Henry Hudson and the Dutch claim to Manhattan
segments.summary: Henry Hudson, an English explorer working for the Dutch, searched for a northeast passage to China, discovered the Hudson River, and found Manhattan. The Dutch West India Company then established New Netherland.

segments.title: Peter Minuit and the purchase of Manhattan
segments.summary: Peter Minuit allegedly bought Manhattan from local Native Americans for goods valued at sixty guilders, as recorded in his letter. The hosts discuss the Manhattan name legend, the mismatch in land ownership concepts, the disputed value of the trade goods, and later Native land sales in Manhattan and Brooklyn.

segments.title: Nutmeg, the Banda Islands and Run
segments.summary: Nutmeg is described as a valuable spice found only in the Banda Islands. The Dutch established a monopoly, brutalized the local population, and imported colonists. The British held Run, and the Dutch tried to stop nutmeg cultivation elsewhere by dipping seeds in lime. Commander Jan Pieterszoon Coen burned nutmeg trees despite a cooperation agreement with England.

segments.title: Treaties trading Manhattan for Run
segments.summary: The Dutch lost Manhattan to England in 1664 with little resistance. The Treaty of Breda in 1667 gave England Manhattan in exchange for keeping the Dutch Run island and nutmeg. The Dutch retook Manhattan in 1673 before the Treaty of Westminster in 1674 returned it.

segments.title: Robert De Niro tipping story
segments.summary: A listener named Corey Osborne recounts Robert De Niro tipping bellmen and a doorman at the Fairmont Washington, D.C. hotel after a checkout.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck mention the Literary Pub Crawl and ask for listener feedback and then sign off.
